decisions.reason: The merged sentence preserves the horn’s unintelligible call and the will-or-instinct question.
The question from BASE is preserved in H001; ordinary will-versus-instinct here does not invoke the glossary’s system attribute.
The flash is retained in H004, so deleting the standalone sentence avoids duplication without dropping the image.
The flash and the enemy falling beneath the gleaming sword are both preserved.
SOL changes the subject: it is the movements carved into his body that trace the precise path, not explicitly his sword.
“Into his attacker’s side” naturally conveys the source’s stab into the flank while preserving the reverse grip.
The death rattle is retained in H008 as the dying groan reaching his ears.
The merged passage preserves the groan, the sword pulled from the chest, and Mukyung rushing toward another enemy.
The action of racing toward another target is retained in H008; this line preserves the striking closed-eyes detail.
The sense of feeling everything without sight is retained in H011.
The merged phrasing preserves both his ability to feel without seeing and the heightened vividness with his eyes closed.
The two years in total darkness are retained in H013.
The merged passage preserves the duration, pitch-black darkness, and why he swung his sword.
SOL keeps the sharpened senses and leap in Qi Sense while expressing the passage naturally.
The grisly sound cuts off the shout, and the repeated enemy kills and ragged breathing remain intact.
His dizziness is retained at the start of H017.
The merged line preserves his dizziness, waterlogged heaviness, and dreamlike haze.
“The fight” preserves the encounter with the Demon Bird and the moment of enlightenment.
The organs and acupoints are still twisted and torn, with their pain vividly conveyed.
The framing that Mukyung knows is retained in H022.
The near-miraculous victory over the Demon Bird is retained in H022.
The merged passage preserves the near-miracle, their life-risking help, the hard-to-repeat strike, and the divine weapon against Force.
The divine weapon capable of standing up to Force is retained in H022.
“The Demon Bird would be standing here instead of him” preserves the counterfactual outcome.
Swallowing the blood and drawing breath are retained in H026.
The merged line preserves the blood, breath, slipping hilt, surrounding enemies, and their fear and rage.
The faint voice beyond the battle noise remains; “also” adds no necessary meaning.
SOL drops the source’s characterization of the voice as elderly.
The blood-stained vision and both injured men gasping on one knee are preserved.
“Laughed at the resolve in his voice” preserves the response to Mukyung’s firm reply.
The teasing reference to the Jin Family’s stubbornness and the cut-off speech remain.
The sound effect conveys the blood pattering down as Wipeng coughs.
The cough and Mukyung’s darkening gaze are preserved; the patter is conveyed in H032.
The information about blood’s color and contents is retained in H035.
The merged passage preserves how the blood indicates severity and the miracle that Wipeng remains conscious.
The bucketfuls-to-handful exaggeration remains clear in Wipeng’s dialogue.
The casual delivery, his awareness of the danger, and his struggle to keep his eyes open are preserved.
The interrupted plea to save his strength is preserved in natural dialogue.
The sudden rigidity and Wipeng’s bloodstained smile remain intact.
“You know what’s best” naturally preserves the claim that all three know the best choice.
The name is clear from the scene, and Mukyung’s clenched teeth are preserved.
The source first affirms that they can return; SOL changes this to Mukyung alone, anticipating and disrupting the next line’s reveal.
Wipeng’s gentle attribution is supplied naturally in H042.
SOL omits the crucial condition that Mukyung can return only if he goes alone.
Breaking through preserves the stated escape route without requiring the redundant phrase “make your escape.”
The right choice and costly mistake are retained in H047.
The merged passage preserves the tactical choice, its cost, and the hundreds of enemies waiting to strike.
Both the old tiger’s former command of Mount Heng and the Peak swordsman’s ghostly swordplay remain.
The broken claws and swordplay lost with the shattered arm are preserved.
“Terrorized an age” changes the source’s description of a fiend who once held sway over an era.
SOL drops the emphasis in “you, at least, must live”—the point that Mukyung above all needs to survive.
The fragment continues the prior line naturally and preserves that his family rank is not the reason.
“Ready to close forever” implies permanent death; the source describes eyes about to go dark.
The assertion that the youth is not simply Mukyung is retained in H055.
The merged passage preserves the shift from Mukyung’s identity to hope and future revenge.
“Whatever it takes” preserves the command to survive by any means.
The return to both the speakers and their enemies is preserved.
The recurring seasons and the disappearance of people are preserved in natural English.
Wipeng’s belief and Cheol Mubaek’s certainty are retained in H061.
The winter returning to their enemies is retained in H061.
The combined passage preserves both the winter image and Mukyung’s future role in bringing them down.
Wipeng’s faint smile toward Mukyung is retained in H063.
Wipeng’s remembered image of Mukyung as a boy asking for sword lessons is preserved.
“At once” preserves the urgency of leaving right now.
“Superior in the family” naturally conveys the source’s senior position.
The name is clear in context, and his speechlessness and shut eyes remain.
The statement that he knew is retained in H068.
The source says what he must do to save more people; “the most people” changes that quantity to a maximum.
“Would not move” preserves the inability to take a step.
The remembered lesson from when he first took up a sword is preserved without unnecessary name repetition.
The teaching to overcome the strong and help the weak is retained in H072.
Standing against the strong, helping the weak, opposing injustice, and keeping faith preserve the teaching.
“Claimed to stand for what was right” adds skepticism absent from the source’s description of an orthodox martial artist’s duty.
SOL drops the source’s explicit “meaning” of the two words, retaining only their weight.
“What’s best?” preserves the question in idiomatic direct thought.
The source says Wipeng and Cheol Mubaek stated the question; SOL incorrectly says they asked it.
The sudden realization is preserved, and Mukyung is unambiguous in context.
Pressing his foot into the ground preserves the source’s action of setting his foot down.
The sword tip’s former trembling and its unwavering aim are preserved.
The inclusive phrasing naturally retains the warning not to forget what is right.
The cautious approach, diagonal torso cut, and blade slicing through the spear are preserved.
The shortened spoken question preserves the source’s meaning.
The flowing movement and blue Sword Energy infused with the fleeting insight remain.
The three Keshik, single stroke, crescent saber, and throw are all preserved.
“What choice won’t I regret?” preserves the direct question about avoiding regret.
“Too quickly for a scream” adds a speed-based explanation absent from the source’s image of death without a scream.
The archer’s fall signals the surrounding enemies’ simultaneous charge, fear, and rage.
“Gleamed” preserves the flashes in the darkness.
SOL changes the glossary term from “throwing blades” to “flying blade” and shifts roughly ten weapons to more than a dozen.
The abrupt “Heat” preserves the sensation and the blood mingling with the wind.
The source says he could avoid the attacks; “knew how to avoid” changes ability into knowledge.
The self-directed disappointment and anger are retained in H093.
The merged line preserves his shame and the brief temptation to choose what was best over what was right.
His cleared thoughts and clenched teeth are preserved.
The source says the smell of blood filled his mouth; SOL changes smell to taste.
The pain displacing pain and his consciousness returning are preserved.
The blue Sword Energy gathering from small waves is retained at the start of H098.
The merged passage preserves the energy’s gathering, its response to the swordsman’s will, and the beautiful arc.
The perfect arc and the dead fiend’s likely laughter remain.
“Cold edge” replaces the source’s chill as the thing cleaving through the darkness, changing the image.
The ten Keshik leaders charge at Mukyung and open their eyes wide in unison.
Their realization is retained at the start of H103.
The merged passage preserves what the Demon Bird saw and what the powerful martial monster felt.
The monster’s experience is retained in H103.
Both sets of weapons groaning under their tangible energy are preserved.
The fading weapon energy, broken prized weapons, and tilting vision remain intact.
The Korean describes a dense or deep fountain of blood, not a dark one.
“A single blue wave of a strike” muddles the source’s comparison: the strike itself is like a blue wave.
The murmuring is retained with the dialogue, avoiding a separate redundant sentence.
Remembering the old fiend as the strike’s first prey, Mukyung steps toward the frozen enemies.
The transition at that moment is preserved.
SOL preserves both parts of the question: who the promise was to and what was promised.
Mukyung’s whole body going rigid is preserved without needless name repetition.
The unfamiliar voice comes from a man standing close by and looking at him.
The shouted call erupts from every direction and drowns out Mukyung’s voice.
The contrast between an unfamiliar voice and a familiar name is preserved.
SOL restricts “the strongest nomad warrior” to the vanguard, while the source identifies him as the strongest nomad warrior.
The curse’s threat and list of family, friends, and home remain; the punctuation preserves its force.
The final face-to-face realization is retained in H120.
The merged passage preserves his recognition of Jamukha and the lack of exaggeration in the curse.
“The Sword Demon” naturally preserves the identification by title.
The ruler’s step toward Mukyung is preserved without unnecessary name repetition.
“Faint but unmistakable” preserves the tremor’s smallness and clarity.
